component_findings.async_structured: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Asynchronous concurrency has first-class composition and structured lifetime/join/cancellation mechanisms or an equivalent disciplined model. Evidence basis: Kotlin | Kotlin's core concurrency model is structured concurrency via coroutines: suspend functions, CoroutineScope, Job hierarchies, and cancellation propagate automatically through parent/child scopes, which is a language/library-level (not just runtime) design feature baked into the type system (suspend modifier) and standard library (kotlinx.coroutines is the de-facto standard, though technically a library not the language core). | Structured concurrency gives compile-time-checked suspension points (suspend keyword) preventing accidental blocking calls in non-blocking contexts, and coroutine cancellation/exception propagation is well-defined (SupervisorJob vs Job semantics, CancellationException handling). | Coroutines are lightweight (many thousands can run on a small thread pool via dispatchers: Dispatchers.Default/IO/Main), giving cheap concurrency without OS-thread-per-task overhead, comparable in spirit to Go's goroutines though implemented via CPS-transformed suspend functions rather than a runtime-managed stack-switching scheduler. | Structured primitives: async/await (via async{} + await()), select{} expressions for multiplexing channels/deferreds, Channel/Flow for producer-consumer and reactive streams, Mutex for coroutine-safe locking — a fairly complete and coherent toolkit comparable to or exceeding Java's traditional java.util.concurrent while staying more com…

component_findings.abi_calling_control: Recertified level 3 under the current criterion: ABI/calling-convention/linkage choices are explicit or safely standardized for common interoperability cases. Evidence basis: Kotlin | Kotlin/JVM interoperates directly and bidirectionally with Java: any Java library, class, or interface can be called with essentially zero-cost, idiomatic syntax (no wrapper generation step), and Kotlin classes are usable from Java with @JvmStatic/@JvmOverloads/@JvmName annotations for ergonomic exposure. | Kotlin/Native exposes a C interop tool (cinterop) that consumes .def files describing a C header and generates Kotlin bindings; this supports calling native C libraries but requires an extra build-time codegen step and .def authoring, unlike Java interop which is seamless. | Kotlin/Native can also export its own APIs to C via generated headers for embedding in C/C++/Swift/Obj-C hosts (used heavily for Kotlin Multiplatform iOS targets), giving two-way native interop, but the calling-convention and memory-model bridging (Kotlin/Native's object model, refcounting, frozen/thread-affinity rules pre-1.7.20) adds real cognitive and correctness overhead absent from the JVM path. | There is no equivalent of Rust's zero-overhead #[repr(C)] + extern "C" direct ABI compatibility, nor Zig's seamless direct C-header inclusion; Kotlin's non-JVM native interop is mediated through generated bindings and runtime shims. | JNI is still needed for JVM-side calls into native code (Kotlin does not remove this JVM/native boundary cost); Project Panama/Foreign Function Interface adoption in…
